w: Locals call it the UFO Bridge for the saucer-shaped structure atop its single pylon. An asymmetrical cable-stayed span across the Danube, its cables anchor to a tower on the Petrzalka side alone -- a main span of 303 metres, the world's longest bridge on just one pylon and cable plane.
s: one pylon holding up a UFO
_facts: Known as 'Most SNP' or the 'UFO Bridge'
Asymmetrical cable-stayed bridge, main span 303m
World's longest single-pylon, single-cable-plane bridge
Four traffic lanes upper deck, bike/pedestrian lanes lower deck

w: A Rococo, late-Baroque summer palace on Hodzovo Square, complete with a French formal garden behind it. It now serves as the official residence of the President of Slovakia -- a head of state working next door to the country's other grand 18th-century leftover, the Episcopal Summer Palace.
s: a Rococo garden for Slovakia's president
_facts: Rococo (late Baroque) summer palace with French garden
Situated on Hodzovo Square
Official residence of the President of Slovakia

w: Built 1778-81 for Jozsef Batthyany, Archbishop of Esztergom and Primate of Hungary, this neoclassical palace's Hall of Mirrors hosted the signing of the fourth Peace of Pressburg in 1805, ending the War of the Third Coalition. Today it's the seat of Bratislava's mayor -- a working city hall with a treaty-making past.
s: a peace treaty signed under a Hall of Mirrors
_facts: Built 1778-1781, designed by Melchior Hefele
Built for Archbishop Jozsef Batthyany
Hall of Mirrors: fourth Peace of Pressburg signed here 1805
Today the seat of the Mayor of Bratislava

w: A 196-metre transmission mast on Kamzik hill, 437 metres above sea level in the Little Carpathians, replacing an older tower when it went up in 1975. Its public observation deck looks out over Bratislava Forest Park and, on a clear day, across the borders into Austria, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
s: on a clear day, three countries at once
_facts: 196m tall, built 1975, replacing an earlier tower
Sits at 437m elevation on Kamzik hill
Has a public observation deck
On clear days, Austria, Hungary and Czech Republic are visible

w: A 17th-century Renaissance summer seat built for the Archbishops of Esztergom, who relocated here after Ottoman forces occupied Esztergom in 1543. The Baroque sculptor Georg Rafael Donner kept a studio in its garden for nearly a decade. These days the palace houses the government of Slovakia.
s: a Baroque sculptor's studio in the garden
_facts: 17th-century Renaissance summer palace for Archbishops of Esztergom
Archbishops based here after Esztergom fell to the Ottomans in 1543
Sculptor Georg Rafael Donner had a studio in the garden for ~10 years
Now houses the Slovak government

w: A Roman frontier camp built in the 2nd century, part of Pannonia's defence line, abandoned when the legions withdrew in the 4th. Behind Rusovce's Catholic church, its remains -- a 30-by-30-metre building with 2.4-metre walls, plus gravestones and ceramic finds -- form a summer museum, added to the UNESCO list in 2021.
s: a 2nd-century Roman fort behind the church
_facts: Roman military camp, built 2nd century, part of Pannonia
Abandoned in the 4th century when legions withdrew
Best-preserved structure: 30x30m building, 2.4m-thick walls
Added to UNESCO World Heritage List 2021 (Danubian Limes)

w: A long, tree-lined square in the Old Town, running between the Novy Most bridge and the Slovak National Theatre. It's named for Pavol Orszagh Hviezdoslav, the national poet -- a literary namesake for what's now one of Bratislava's most-walked stretches of pavement, framed by two of the city's biggest landmarks.
s: the poet's square between bridge and theatre
_facts: Town square in the Old Town of Bratislava
Located between Novy Most bridge and the Slovak National Theatre
Named after poet Pavol Orszagh Hviezdoslav

w: Slovakia's second-largest gallery of its kind, split between the Mirbach Palace and the Palffy Palace in the Old Town. Founded in 1961 -- though the city had been collecting since the 19th century -- it now holds around 35,000 works of art across the two historic buildings.
_facts: Second-largest Slovak gallery of its kind
Housed in Mirbach Palace and Palffy Palace
Founded 1961, roots in 19th-century collecting
Around 35,000 works in its collection

w: Built in the 1870s near the Danube riverfront, reconstructed twice over -- in the 1920s and again in the 1950s -- to fit it for its current job housing exhibitions of the Slovak National Gallery. Modern extensions and the adjoining Water Barracks have since folded it into a much larger museum campus.
s: a Neo-Renaissance shell for the national gallery
_facts: Neo-Renaissance building built in the 1870s
Reconstructed in the 1920s and 1950s
Adapted for the Slovak National Gallery
Now linked to the Water Barracks and modern extensions

w: Built in 1661 for Countess Frances, widow of Paul Palffy, this early Baroque church replaced a Gothic predecessor on the same spot below Bratislava Castle. It's dedicated to St. Nicholas, patron of sailors, whose statue watches from a niche above the door -- a small, protected landmark in the castle's shadow.
s: an Orthodox chapel for a castle-hill widow
_facts: Built 1661 by Countess Frances, widow of Paul Palffy
Early Baroque, replaced an earlier Gothic church on the site
Dedicated to St. Nicholas, patron saint of sailors
Protected cultural monument

w: One of two squares that argue over being Bratislava's true centre, fronting the Grassalkovich Palace just steps from the Old Town. Its fountain, Earth - planet of peace, is the city's default meeting point, sitting above underpasses of shops built in the 1970s -- a transport hub as much as a public square.
s: the fountain everyone in Bratislava meets at
_facts: Major square at the edge of the Old Town
Fronts the Grassalkovich Palace
Considered one of the two centres of Bratislava
Fountain 'Earth - planet of peace' is a common meeting point

w: Laid out in 1774-76 with allees fanning out in an eight-legged star, each named for its tree, this is one of the oldest public parks in Europe. Its Gothic tower -- remnant of a 15th-century Franciscan church, rebuilt Neogothic after an 1897 earthquake -- still rises over Janko Kral's statue among the trees.
s: one of Europe's oldest municipal parks
_facts: Established 1774-76, among Europe's oldest municipal parks
Star-shaped layout of tree-named allees
Gothic tower is remnant of a 15th-century Franciscan church
Tower damaged by 1897 earthquake, rebuilt Neogothic

w: An early Baroque chapel built at the end of the 17th century in Lamac, then its own village on Bratislava's edge. Protected as a national cultural landmark since 1963, it's one of the last physical witnesses to how Lamac looked and was built before the city swallowed it -- still owned by Bratislava today.
_facts: Early Baroque chapel, built late 17th century
Located in Lamac, once a separate village
Slovak national cultural landmark, protected since 1963
Owned by the city of Bratislava

w: A massive rectangular fortress with four corner towers, planted on an isolated rock above the Danube -- impossible to miss from almost anywhere in the city. On a clear day the views reach into Austria and Hungary. Centuries of legend have attached themselves to it, as they tend to with a castle this dominant.
s: four towers, one rock, centuries of legend
_facts: Rectangular building with four corner towers
Stands on an isolated rocky hill above the Danube
Views extend to Austria and, in clear weather, Hungary
Many legends connected with its history
